blocks.text: Preserve an Entire Line

A label such as North courtyard is a single piece of data even though it contains two words. std::getline(entrada, linea) reads characters until a newline. It stores them in a std::string, consumes the newline that terminates the line, and does not include it in the destination. Unlike >> for strings, it preserves leading, internal, and trailing spaces.

std::getline receives the stream first and then the destination. It returns the stream so you can check the read in a condition. The function is declared in <string>; a prepared text stream still needs <sstream>. These labs do not read from the keyboard.

The first line retains its two leading and two trailing spaces. The second is read even though the text ends without another newline. Each loop-body execution corresponds to a successfully read line; the later attempt that cannot read a new line does not execute the body.
An Empty Line Can Be Valid Data

If the next character is a newline, getline consumes it and obtains an empty string. That read succeeds: an empty line was present. If there are no characters or delimiters left to consume, the attempt to read another line fails. Read success and line content are different questions.

blocks.text: linea.empty() asks whether the string contains zero characters. It does not ask whether the stream failed. A line containing two spaces has two characters and is not empty, even if it appears blank without delimiters.

blocks.question: The prepared text is "\n". How many times does while (std::getline(entrada, linea)) execute?
options: Never: an empty string always indicates a failed read.
Once: it obtains a valid empty line terminated by the available newline.
Twice: once for the newline and once for the end of the text.
blocks.explanation: The newline permits a valid empty line. The following attempt finds no characters or further delimiter, so it ends the loop.

blocks.text: Combining Reading Rules Requires Knowing What Remains

>> stops reading a word when it reaches whitespace and does not consume that final delimiter as part of the word. An immediate getline starts exactly where that operation stopped; it may encounter the newline still waiting there. No new line was skipped: the remainder of the current line was read.

In this format, the first getline consumes the empty remainder of the start line; the second obtains Green workshop. If the format were start notice\nGreen workshop, the remainder would contain the leading space and notice. Discarding it without checking would conceal data. First decide what the format permits and then what to do with that remainder.

blocks.question: A format requires preserving an empty line before the label. What is the risk of indiscriminately removing all whitespace before getline?
options: No line can be lost: newlines are not whitespace.
Losing the label's first word, because skipping whitespace also consumes that word.
Losing empty lines that are part of the data.
blocks.explanation: Newlines are whitespace too. Removing all of them makes a meaningful empty line disappear before the read meant to preserve it. Skipping whitespace does not read a word: it stops at the first non-whitespace character.

blocks.text: Separate the Source from Its Meaning

getline decides where a line ends; it does not check whether its contents match the format required by the problem. A line such as add three might have been read successfully and still be an invalid command. Later, we will put a line that was read into another istringstream to parse its components while preserving the operation boundary.

blocks.question: You want to preserve each line's complete label and then analyze it separately. What is the responsibility of the initial read?
options: Obtain a valid line and preserve its characters for later analysis.
Accept any text as a correct command because getline succeeded.
Automatically convert every word in the line to a number.
blocks.explanation: Line reading obtains a unit of text. Validating its structure and converting its parts are later responsibilities.
